newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria parliament passes new banking law.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria parliament passes new banking law.

text.p: Bulgaria's parliament on Wednesday gave the final blessing to a new banking law aimed to clean up the crumbling banking sector.
"This law, along with the central bank law (voted
earlier) is designed to put the banking system back on track and lays the foundation for stabilisation," head of parliament's budget and finance committee Yordan Tsonev told the assembly.

The law, part of preparations to launch the currency board system on July 1, aims to strengthen bank supervision and minimise risk of bank failures, he added. Seventeen Bulgarian banks - a third of their total number -- are now in receivership and their closures are sought by the central bank through courts.

The law, due to come in force after being published in the State Gazette, raises the capital requirements for bank licensing to 10 billion levs ($5.9 million) from 2.2 billion levs. The capital must be cash rather than securities as allowed by the previous law, which led to creation of numerous weak banks.
The new law requires banks to disclose account information to the police and National Investigation Service on companies with state or municipal majority participation.
Banks are also required to publish balance sheets every six months. Loans and interest which are 90 days overdue are excluded from the assets until they are paid back.

Loans which are not paid on the due date can be collected with a court order, the law says. So far banks could only sue their debtors, which took years under the cumbersome local legal system. The law requires banks to participate in a deposit guarantee fund.

Banks can not remain in receivership longer than two months after the new law is enacted if the central bank has not revoked their licenses. Very few of the banks placed in receivership had their licenses retracted so far.
Central bank restrictions and license withdrawals cannot be appealed in court. The law would also annul all appeals filed so far.
The law was approved as part of measures setting the stage for the currency board system, a restrictive monetary regime involving rigid money supply control and fixed exchange rate.
The 1997 budget is the last of laws parliament needs to finalise before the start of the currency board.
